checkpoints: Constructing a new Redis client with `new Redis(...)` inside every request handler opens a fresh TCP connection and performs a full Redis handshake on every single call, instead of reusing one connection across requests.

At high request volume — thousands of location pings per second — that per-call connection cost exhausts the process's available file descriptors or Redis's own `maxclients` ceiling long before the service becomes CPU-bound.

The correct pattern is a single shared `ioredis` client built once behind a DI provider (bound to a token such as `REDIS_CLIENT`) and injected into the service's constructor, so one durable connection is reused and pipelines commands for the entire app lifetime.

A Redis sorted set used for `GEOADD` has no concept of per-member expiry, so a driver's coordinate remains in the `drivers:geo` key indefinitely once written, even after that driver goes offline or the process crashes mid-shift.

Without a cleanup mechanism the GEO key only grows over time, turning into a big key and becoming a source of ghost matches — nearby-driver results that still include drivers who are no longer actually online.

Filtering stale drivers at query time, such as checking a heartbeat key with `EXISTS`, hides ghost entries from the API response but does not shrink the underlying sorted set, so a periodic sweeper job is still needed to actively `ZREM` expired members and keep the key's size bounded.

A test suite that exercises only a single driver doing one write and one read at low load cannot expose either defect, because connection exhaustion and unbounded key growth only manifest once concurrency or driver churn crosses a volume the tests never approach, so a green suite proves nothing about production readiness.

Proving the fix actually works requires a soak test under sustained load with drivers cycling online and offline, asserting that both the process's open-connection count and the GEO key's member count stay flat over time instead of climbing.

A document in this BM25 index is represented in two places at once: the record itself in `docs`, and scattered traces of it across the posting list of every term it once contained in `postings`. Deleting only from `docs` leaves the second representation completely untouched.

When a deleted document's id is left inside a term's posting list, that document can still be pulled into the scoring loop the next time the term is queried — `termFrequency` resolves to 0 once `docs.get(id)` is undefined, so the entry scores 0, but the id can still surface in the returned result set.

IDF's document-frequency count `n` is computed from the size of a term's posting list, so leaving a deleted document's id inside every posting list it belonged to keeps `n` artificially inflated — this understates IDF for that term for every OTHER still-valid document, not just the deleted one.

A term whose only owning document gets deleted becomes orphaned: its posting list is never emptied and the term key is never removed from `postings`, so `vocabSize` never shrinks even though the live corpus has actually gotten smaller.

Decrementing `N` without also subtracting the deleted document's length from `totalLength`/`docLengths` makes `avgdl` (totalLength / N) drift upward, which skews the BM25 length-normalization term for every remaining document on every subsequent query — not just ones touching the deleted document's terms.

This kind of bug is insidious because nothing throws and `search` keeps returning results that look plausible; the corruption is a silent, gradual degradation of ranking quality rather than an immediate, visible failure.

A correct delete must read the document's `content` and re-tokenize it BEFORE removing it from `docs`, since that is the only place the content still exists — this recovers exactly which terms the document contributed so each one's posting list can be cleaned up.

For each recovered term, a correct delete removes the document's id from that term's posting list, and if the list becomes empty as a result, removes the term key from `postings` entirely — only after posting-list cleanup and length-stat updates are complete should `docs.delete(id)` and the `N` decrement happen, since all of postings, docLengths, totalLength, and N must move together.

Correctness can be proven with a concrete test: index two documents sharing one term plus a third document that owns a term uniquely, delete the document with the unique term, then assert that term is gone from `postings`, `vocabSize` dropped by exactly one, and the remaining documents' scores shift to reflect the freshly recomputed IDF and avgdl.

Serializing the entire in-memory index to a single JSON blob on every mutation makes write cost proportional to the total index size rather than to the size of the change — adding one token still walks every term's posting list and every document record, so cost is O(index size) per write instead of O(delta size).

This pattern is write amplification: as the corpus grows, each small addDocument or removeDocument call pays the full-corpus serialization cost, so both CPU spent in JSON.stringify and bytes written to Redis scale with corpus size rather than with how much actually changed, causing throughput to collapse under high-ingest load even though individual writes are tiny.

The fix is to stop rewriting the whole snapshot on every mutation and instead persist only the delta — appending an operation-log entry (or a small immutable segment) per mutation — and reserve the full compacted snapshot write for a slower background schedule, so a write's cost becomes proportional to the mutation rather than to the whole index.

One incremental approach is an append-only log: push just `{ op, id, content? }` onto a Redis stream on each mutation (cheap, O(1) per write), then periodically or once the log passes a size threshold, run a full serialize-and-set to compact it; on boot, load the last full snapshot and replay the log entries after it to reconstruct an identical index.

An alternative is the Lucene segment model, where each batch of mutations becomes a new small immutable JSON segment, a background job periodically merges old segments together, and boot reads every live segment to rebuild the index.

Incremental or segment-based persistence trades away simplicity for performance: it introduces compaction/merge logic and crash-recovery bookkeeping (e.g., handling a process dying mid-append or mid-segment-write) and tombstone handling for updates/deletes, whereas the single full-snapshot write is simpler and always internally consistent — a reasonable choice for a single-node, low-ingest, or teaching-scale service.

The choice between full-snapshot and incremental persistence should be driven by ingest rate and corpus size, not treated as a correctness bug versus a solution — full-snapshot writes are a deliberate simplification whose acceptability shrinks as ingest rate and corpus size grow.

Verifying the fix requires benchmarking write latency and CPU against corpus size before (expected linear growth) and after the change (expected flat/constant cost), plus a restart or rebuild test asserting the reconstructed index is identical to the one that existed before restart.

When two upstream calls are independent — the second call's input doesn't depend on the first call's output — awaiting them sequentially (`await fetchRanked(bm25); await fetchRanked(vector)`) makes total latency the sum of both engines' latencies instead of the max, even though nothing in the business logic required that ordering.

Firing the two upstream calls concurrently with `Promise.all([fetchRanked(bm25Url, ...), fetchRanked(vectorUrl, ...)])` collapses total latency from bm25Latency + vectorLatency down to roughly max(bm25Latency, vectorLatency), since both calls are now in flight at the same time.

`Promise.all` alone does not bound the tail: it still resolves only once every promise in the array settles, so a single hung engine still pins the whole request — just with a lower floor than before, since the other branch is no longer adding on top of it.

Bounding the tail requires a timeout on each upstream call individually, not just on the aggregate: wrapping each `fetchRanked` call in an `AbortController`, calling `controller.abort()` from a `setTimeout`, and passing `{ signal: controller.signal }` into `fetch` causes that specific call to reject with an `AbortError` once its own budget expires.

A timed-out call should degrade to an empty result list — for example via `.catch(() => [])` on that branch — rather than letting the `AbortError` propagate and fail the whole request; this reuses the same failure-isolation path already used for a genuinely dead upstream, so RRF fuses whatever results did come back.
Because BM25 and vector search are independent engines with no ordering dependency between them, running their calls in parallel is safe and introduces no new race condition or correctness risk.

The `limit * 2` over-fetch is a separate, orthogonal concern from latency — it exists to protect ranking quality (making sure a consensus document survives fusion) and doesn't need to change as part of a latency fix.

Correctness of the fix should be verified two ways: confirming p99 drops to roughly max(bm25Latency, vectorLatency) after parallelizing, and injecting an artificially slow or non-resolving engine to confirm the request still returns within the timeout window with partial results instead of hanging.

On the index path, `tokenize()` normalizes text by lowercasing it and splitting on runs of non-alphanumeric characters, so a document containing "Redis" ends up stored under the key `redis` in `this.postings`.

`queryTokenize()` was added later, lives only inside the query handler, and does not reuse `tokenize()` — it merely splits on whitespace and keeps the original case, so the same word can produce a different token depending on which of the two paths processed it.

Because the query token `Redis` and the indexed key `redis` differ only in case, `this.postings.get(term)` returns undefined for a document that genuinely contains the word — the index path and query path have silently drifted out of sync with each other.

A Map lookup miss is not an error condition in JavaScript/TypeScript, it simply returns undefined, so the `if (!posting) continue` guard skips the term without throwing or logging anything, which makes an empty or partial result look like a legitimate "no match" rather than exposing the bug.

Two independent tokenization implementations that are supposed to agree but are edited separately have no crash-shaped failure signature, so an empty result set with zero exceptions is itself the diagnostic clue pointing at a normalization mismatch between index-time and query-time processing, not a BM25 scoring defect.

The correct fix is to delete `queryTokenize()` entirely and call the same `tokenize()` function from `search()`, guaranteeing the index path and query path always normalize text identically and can never diverge again.

After the fix, re-running the query `Redis` (different case than the stored `redis`) should return the previously missing document, and a regression test asserting that index-time and query-time tokenization produce identical tokens for the same input guards against a future edit to only one of the two paths reintroducing the bug.

This failure mode generalizes beyond casing: any asymmetric normalization step applied on only one of the two paths — a stemmer, a stopword filter, synonym expansion — produces the same silent, exception-free recall collapse, so the durable fix is a single shared normalization pipeline rather than a patch for the specific case difference.
